pos: n. (wasting; want of flesh; a soul made thin; Hebrew razon, razeh)
etymology: From lean, Old English hlæne, thin, wanting flesh. Scripture uses it for the body wasting and, more terribly, for the soul.
biblical_def: Leanness is emptiness that shows. Job sees it as an accuser: “And thou hast filled me with wrinkles, which is a witness against me: and my leanness rising up in me beareth witness to my face” (Job 16:8). But the gravest use in Scripture is not of the body at all. Of Israel in the wilderness, demanding flesh to eat, the psalmist writes: “And he gave them their request; but sent leanness into their soul” (Psa 106:15). That is the whole doctrine of answered prayer in half a verse. God can grant a request as a judgment. Isaiah applies the word to Assyria's glory: “Therefore shall the Lord, the Lord of hosts, send among his fat ones leanness; and under his glory he shall kindle a burning like the burning of a fire” (Isa 10:16). And the prophet takes it on himself in a cry that stands almost alone in the canon for sheer weight: “But I said, My leanness, my leanness, woe unto me!” (Isa 24:16). Fatness in Scripture is not gluttony but abundance and blessing; leanness is its withdrawal. The soul can starve at a full table.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines leanness as destitution of fat; want of flesh; thinness of body; and figuratively, want of matter, poverty, emptiness.
webster_full: LEANNESS, n. Destitution of fat; want of flesh; thinness of body; meagerness.
2. Want of matter; poverty; emptiness; as the leanness of a purse.
LEAN, a. Wanting flesh; meager; not fat; thin.
scriptures: Job 16:8
And thou hast filled me with wrinkles, which is a witness against me: and my leanness rising up in me beareth witness to my face.
And he gave them their request; but sent leanness into their soul.
Therefore shall the Lord, the Lord of hosts, send among his fat ones leanness; and under his glory he shall kindle a burning like the burning of a fire.

From the uttermost part of the earth have we heard songs, even glory to the righteous. But I said, My leanness, my leanness, woe unto me! the treacherous dealers have dealt treacherously; yea, the treacherous dealers have dealt very treacherously.
corruption_summary: Answered prayer is treated as proof of God's favour, when Psalm 106 records a request granted and leanness sent with it.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 106:15 is one of the most neglected verses in Scripture and one of the most necessary. Israel wanted flesh; the LORD gave them flesh; and the same sentence reports that He sent leanness into their soul. The prosperity teaching that reads every granted request as divine approval has no place to put this verse. Neither does the softer popular version of it, which assumes that if a door opened the LORD must have wanted us through it. Sometimes the door opens because we would not stop knocking.

The corrective is not to distrust God's generosity but to distrust our appetite. Israel's petition was not for anything wicked in itself — it was for meat. What condemned it was that it despised the manna already given. A soul can be made thin by getting exactly what it asked for, and the wilderness generation is Scripture's standing exhibit.
roots_summary: Hebrew razon (H7332), leanness, wasting; razeh (H7330), lean; the opposite of dashen, fatness, which in Scripture means abundance and blessing.
roots_lines: Hebrew razon (H7332) — leanness, wasting; Psalm 106:15, Isaiah 10:16.
Hebrew kachash (H3585) — leanness, failing; Job 16:8.
Hebrew razi (H7334) — my leanness; Isaiah 24:16, the prophet's cry.
Hebrew nephesh (H5315) — soul; what the leanness of Psalm 106 was sent into.
Hebrew dashen (H1878) — to be fat, to be made rich; the blessing leanness reverses.
usage: “He gave them their request; but sent leanness into their soul” — a granted prayer as judgment.
“My leanness, my leanness, woe unto me” — Isaiah's cry in the midst of songs.
“Therefore shall the Lord, the Lord of hosts, send among his fat ones leanness” — glory withdrawn from Assyria.

pos: n. (decay from within, especially of the bones; Hebrew raqab)
etymology: From rotten, Old Norse rotinn, decayed. Scripture places the decay in the bones — the innermost and strongest part of the frame — where it cannot be seen and cannot be reached.
biblical_def: Rottenness in Scripture is almost always internal and almost always in the bones. Solomon uses it twice in the Proverbs, and both times the outward frame is intact while the core gives way. “A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband: but she that maketh ashamed is as rottenness in his bones” (Pro 12:4). And on the passion that eats a man alive: “A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones” (Pro 14:30). Isaiah turns it on a nation that had every appearance of health: “so their root shall be as rottenness, and their blossom shall go up as dust: because they have cast away the law of the LORD of hosts, and despised the word of the Holy One of Israel” (Isa 5:24). Hosea makes the LORD Himself the agent: “Therefore will I be unto Ephraim as a moth, and to the house of Judah as rottenness” (Hos 5:12). And Habakkuk, hearing what is coming upon his people, feels it in his own frame: “rottenness entered into my bones, and I trembled in myself, that I might rest in the day of trouble” (Hab 3:16). The picture is consistent: what destroys does not always arrive from outside.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rottenness as a state of being decayed; putrefaction; unsoundness; and figuratively, moral corruption within.
webster_full: ROTTENNESS, n. State of being rotten; putrefaction; decay; unsoundness.
ROTTEN, a. Putrid; carious; decomposed by the natural process of decay.
2. Not firm or trusty; unsound; defective in principle; as a rotten heart.
scriptures: Pro 12:4
A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband: but she that maketh ashamed is as rottenness in his bones.
A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones.
Isa 5:24

Therefore as the fire devoureth the stubble, and the flame consumeth the chaff, so their root shall be as rottenness, and their blossom shall go up as dust: because they have cast away the law of the LORD of hosts, and despised the word of the Holy One of Israel.
Hos 5:12
Therefore will I be unto Ephraim as a moth, and to the house of Judah as rottenness.
corruption_summary: Envy is treated as a harmless private feeling, while Proverbs classes it with a disease of the bones.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 14:30 sets two conditions side by side: a sound heart is the life of the flesh, but envy the rottenness of the bones. Modern moral vocabulary has almost no category for envy. It is not litigable, it harms no one visibly, and it can be carried a whole life without confession. Scripture treats it as a wasting disease of the skeleton — the part of a man that holds him up. That is not hyperbole in a book that also says a merry heart doeth good like a medicine.

Hosea 5:12 supplies the fearful half of the doctrine. The LORD says He will be to Judah as rottenness — not as a sword, not as an invading army, but as slow decay. Judgment does not always come as an event. Sometimes it comes as a nation quietly losing the strength it assumes it still has, and the prophets name that as the LORD's own work, not as historical misfortune.
roots_summary: Hebrew raqab (H7538), rottenness, decay of bone or wood; maq (H4716), rot; the figure is fixed to 'etsem, bone, the frame's inmost strength.
roots_lines: Hebrew raqab (H7538) — rottenness; Proverbs 12:4, 14:30, Hosea 5:12.
Hebrew 'etsem (H6106) — bone; the seat of the decay in every proverb.
Hebrew maq (H4716) — rot, decay; Isaiah 5:24, the root as rottenness.
Hebrew qin'ah (H7068) — envy, jealousy; the cause named in Proverbs 14:30.
Hebrew 'ash (H6211) — moth; paired with rottenness in Hosea 5:12.
usage: “Envy the rottenness of the bones” — a private sin classed as skeletal disease.
“Their root shall be as rottenness” — the blossom still showing.
“Therefore will I be unto Ephraim as a moth” — judgment that arrives slowly.

pos: v. (invested with, furnished with a gift from without; Hebrew zabad, Greek enduo)
etymology: From Old French enduire, and touching Latin induere, to put on as a garment. The KJV keeps the passive: a man is never said to endue himself.
biblical_def: Endued is a passive word in Scripture, and the passivity is the doctrine. Leah says, “God hath endued me with a good dowry” (Gen 30:20). Huram writes of Solomon that the LORD “hath given to David the king a wise son, endued with prudence and understanding, that might build an house for the LORD, and an house for his kingdom” (2Ch 2:12), and of his own craftsman, “And now I have sent a cunning man, endued with understanding” (2Ch 2:13). James asks, “Who is a wise man and endued with knowledge among you? let him shew out of a good conversation his works with meekness of wisdom” (Jas 3:13). And the Lord Jesus uses it for the promise that closes Luke's Gospel: “And, behold, I send the promise of my Father upon you: but tarry ye in the city of Jerusalem, until ye be endued with power from on high” (Luk 24:49). In every instance the gift comes from outside the man and is put upon him. The apostles were commanded to wait. They had seen the risen Christ, they had the commission, and they were still told to sit still in Jerusalem until they were clothed with what they did not have.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines endue as to invest, to supply with, to furnish with something as a gift or endowment.
webster_full: ENDUE, v.t. To invest; to supply with; to furnish; as, to endue a man with power or with talents.
ENDUED, pp. Invested; furnished; supplied with.
2. Clothed; as, endued with power from on high.
scriptures: And Leah said, God hath endued me with a good dowry; now will my husband dwell with me, because I have born him six sons: and she called his name Zebulun.

Huram said moreover, Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, that made heaven and earth, who hath given to David the king a wise son, endued with prudence and understanding, that might build an house for the LORD, and an house for his kingdom.
And, behold, I send the promise of my Father upon you: but tarry ye in the city of Jerusalem, until ye be endued with power from on high.
Jas 3:13
Who is a wise man and endued with knowledge among you? let him shew out of a good conversation his works with meekness of wisdom.
corruption_summary: Spiritual power is pursued as a technique to be acquired, when Luke 24 makes it a clothing put on the waiting church from above.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 24:49 governs the word. Tarry ye in the city of Jerusalem, until ye be endued with power from on high. The men who received that order had the fullest credentials in the history of the church — eyewitnesses of the resurrection, personally commissioned — and they were commanded to do nothing. Every method that promises to generate spiritual power by intensity, technique, or the right meeting is answered by that verse. Power from on high is put on; it is not worked up.

The New Apostolic Reformation and its cousins invert this by treating the enduement as a transferable impartation flowing through recognized apostles and prophets. Scripture knows nothing of it. The Spirit is given by the Father through the Son to the church, and the sign of a man endued with knowledge, as James says, is not manifestation but conduct: let him shew out of a good conversation his works with meekness of wisdom.
roots_summary: Greek enduo (G1746), to clothe, to put on — the same verb Paul uses for putting on Christ and the armour of God; Hebrew zabad (H2064), to bestow, endow.
roots_lines: Greek enduo (G1746) — to clothe, to be endued; Luke 24:49.
Greek epistemon (G1990) — knowing, endued with knowledge; James 3:13.
Hebrew zabad (H2064) — to bestow upon; Genesis 30:20, Leah's good dowry.
Hebrew yada' (H3045) — to know; the understanding Huram's craftsman was endued with.
Greek dunamis (G1411) — power; what the church at Jerusalem was to be clothed with.
usage: “Tarry ye in the city of Jerusalem, until ye be endued with power from on high” — wait, then go.
“Endued with prudence and understanding, that might build an house for the LORD” — the gift precedes the work.
“A wise man and endued with knowledge” — proved by conversation, not by claim.

etymology: Latin eminere, to stand out, to project. English has made the word an honour; Ezekiel uses it four times and three of them are an accusation.
biblical_def: In English eminent is a compliment. In Ezekiel it is usually a charge. Of Jerusalem playing the harlot the LORD says, “That thou hast also built unto thee an eminent place, and hast made thee an high place in every street” (Eze 16:24), and again, “In that thou buildest thine eminent place in the head of every way, and makest thine high place in every street” (Eze 16:31). The sentence follows: “And I will also give thee into their hand, and they shall throw down thine eminent place, and shall break down thy high places” (Eze 16:39). Something raised up in the head of every way, visible from every direction, built by the covenant people for a worship the LORD never commanded — that is what eminence means in these chapters. But the word is redeemed one chapter later, and by God Himself: “I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar, and will set it; I will crop off from the top of his young twigs a tender one, and will plant it upon an high mountain and eminent” (Eze 17:22). Israel's self-made eminence is thrown down; the eminence the LORD plants is a tender twig He sets on the mountain Himself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines eminent as high; lofty; exalted in rank or station; conspicuous; distinguished.
webster_full: EMINENT, a. High; lofty; as an eminent place.
2. Exalted in rank; high in office or station; as an eminent statesman.
3. Conspicuous; remarkable; distinguished; as eminent piety or eminent services.
scriptures: That thou hast also built unto thee an eminent place, and hast made thee an high place in every street.
In that thou buildest thine eminent place in the head of every way, and makest thine high place in every street; and hast not been as an harlot, in that thou scornest hire;

And I will also give thee into their hand, and they shall throw down thine eminent place, and shall break down thy high places: they shall strip thee also of thy clothes, and shall take thy fair jewels, and leave thee naked and bare.

Thus saith the Lord GOD; I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar, and will set it; I will crop off from the top of his young twigs a tender one, and will plant it upon an high mountain and eminent:
corruption_summary: Platform and visibility are treated as the measure of ministry, while Ezekiel calls a self-built eminent place in the head of every way a harlotry.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 16 gives the anatomy of religious self-promotion with painful precision: an eminent place, in the head of every way, in every street. The offence is not that worship happened but that Jerusalem chose its own elevation and its own locations. Applied to the present, the rebuke lands on a church culture organized around visibility — where a ministry's standing is measured by reach, and where the platform is built first and the doctrine fitted to it afterward.

Ezekiel 17:22 keeps this from becoming a general suspicion of prominence. The LORD Himself plants a cutting upon an high mountain and eminent, and the Messianic reference is unmistakable: the tender twig becomes a goodly cedar under which all fowl of every wing shall dwell. Eminence is not the sin. Seizing it is. The Son of Man is exalted because the Father plants Him, and Philippians 2 puts the order beyond dispute — He humbled Himself, wherefore God hath highly exalted Him.
roots_summary: Hebrew gab (H1354), a mound or elevated place; talul (H8524), lofty, exalted, of the mountain where the LORD plants His branch; bamah (H1116), the high place of false worship.
roots_lines: Hebrew gab (H1354) — eminent place, mound; Ezekiel 16:24, 16:31, 16:39.
Hebrew bamah (H1116) — high place; paired with the eminent place in every verse of Ezekiel 16.
Hebrew talul (H8524) — lofty, eminent; Ezekiel 17:22, the mountain the LORD chooses.
Hebrew gaboah (H1364) — high; the cedar from which the tender twig is cropped.
Hebrew rosh (H7218) — head, top; in the head of every way, Ezekiel 16:31.
usage: “Thou hast also built unto thee an eminent place” — self-chosen elevation.
“They shall throw down thine eminent place” — what is seized is taken.
“I will crop off from the top of his young twigs a tender one, and will plant it upon an high mountain and eminent” — what God plants stands.

pos: adj. (of one's own will; freely offered; Hebrew nedabah, Greek thelo)
etymology: Latin voluntas, will. In Leviticus it describes an offering nobody compelled; in Colossians it describes a religion nobody commanded.
biblical_def: Voluntary cuts two ways in Scripture and the difference is everything. In the law it marks the willingness of a commanded offering: “he shall offer it of his own voluntary will at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation before the LORD” (Lev 1:3), and it names a class of sacrifice, “But if the sacrifice of his offering be a vow, or a voluntary offering, it shall be eaten the same day that he offereth his sacrifice” (Lev 7:16). Ezekiel's prince does the same in the restored temple: “Now when the prince shall prepare a voluntary burnt offering or peace offerings voluntarily unto the LORD, one shall then open him the gate that looketh toward the east” (Eze 46:12). Here voluntary means the heart is in it — the form is God's, the willingness is the worshipper's. But Paul uses the same English word for something the LORD never asked for: “Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind” (Col 2:18). A voluntary offering within God's ordinance is worship; a voluntary humility outside it is self-will wearing the clothes of devotion.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines voluntary as acting by choice, or proceeding from the will; free; not constrained; done of one's own accord.
webster_full: VOLUNTARY, a. Acting by choice or without being influenced by another; free.
2. Proceeding from choice or free will; as a voluntary offering.
3. Done by design; purposed; intended.
4. Free; open; unconstrained.
scriptures: Lev 1:3
If his offering be a burnt sacrifice of the herd, let him offer a male without blemish: he shall offer it of his own voluntary will at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation before the LORD.
Lev 7:16
But if the sacrifice of his offering be a vow, or a voluntary offering, it shall be eaten the same day that he offereth his sacrifice: and on the morrow also the remainder of it shall be eaten:

Now when the prince shall prepare a voluntary burnt offering or peace offerings voluntarily unto the LORD, one shall then open him the gate that looketh toward the east, and he shall prepare his burnt offering and his peace offerings, as he did on the sabbath day: then he shall go forth; and after his going forth one shall shut the gate.
Col 2:18
Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind,
corruption_summary: Self-chosen devotion is prized as sincerity, while Colossians 2 names voluntary humility as the very engine of will-worship.
corruption_paragraphs: Colossians 2:18 is the New Testament's sharpest statement of what the Reformed tradition calls the regulative principle. Paul is not describing men who worship badly; he is describing men who worship extra — intruding into those things which he hath not seen, and doing it with an air of humility. The next verses call the whole apparatus will-worship, and note that it has indeed a shew of wisdom and is of no value against the indulgence of the flesh. Devotion that the LORD did not ask for is not a lesser obedience; it is a different religion.

Leviticus keeps the balance. God commands the sacrifice and still requires that it be offered of a man's own voluntary will. Grudging obedience is not the alternative to will-worship — free obedience to a commanded form is. The Christian is not asked to choose between a warm heart and a regulated worship; he is given both, and told they belong together.
roots_summary: Hebrew nedabah (H5071), a freewill offering, spontaneous gift; ratson (H7522), acceptance, good pleasure; Greek thelo (G2309), to will, in the compound Paul turns against will-worship.
roots_lines: Hebrew nedabah (H5071) — voluntary offering, freewill gift; Leviticus 7:16, Ezekiel 46:12.
Hebrew ratson (H7522) — of his own voluntary will; Leviticus 1:3.
Greek thelo (G2309) — to will, to be willing; Colossians 2:18.
Greek ethelothreskeia (G1479) — will-worship; Colossians 2:23, the verdict on voluntary humility.
Greek tapeinophrosune (G5012) — humility; genuine in Philippians 2, counterfeit in Colossians 2.
usage: “He shall offer it of his own voluntary will” — commanded form, willing heart.
“A vow, or a voluntary offering” — two ways a free gift was brought.
“A voluntary humility and worshipping of angels” — devotion God never asked for.

pos: n. (the womb; that which first opens to birth; Hebrew rechem)
etymology: Latin matrix, womb, from mater, mother. The KJV uses it in one legal formula, all that openeth the matrix, which fixes the LORD's claim upon the firstborn.
biblical_def: Matrix is the KJV's word for the womb, and it appears almost exclusively in one phrase of covenant law. After the passover the command is given: “That thou shalt set apart unto the LORD all that openeth the matrix, and every firstling that cometh of a beast which thou hast; the males shall be the LORD'S” (Exo 13:12). Its ground is the night of the tenth plague: “therefore I sacrifice to the LORD all that openeth the matrix, being males; but all the firstborn of my children I redeem” (Exo 13:15). The claim is restated without qualification: “All that openeth the matrix is mine; and every firstling among thy cattle, whether ox or sheep, that is male” (Exo 34:19). And the Levites are then taken as the substitute: “And I, behold, I have taken the Levites from among the children of Israel instead of all the firstborn that openeth the matrix among the children of Israel: therefore the Levites shall be mine” (Num 3:12). The doctrine is that the first thing a womb ever yields belongs to God by right, and that Israel keeps its firstborn sons only by redemption — a price paid, a substitute accepted.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines matrix as the womb; the cavity in which the fetus is formed and nourished; and by extension, a mould in which anything is cast or shaped.
webster_full: MATRIX, n. The womb; the cavity in which the fetus of an animal is formed and nourished till its birth.
2. A mold; the cavity in which any thing is formed, and which gives it shape.
3. In mining, the earthy or stony substance in which metallic ores are found.
scriptures: That thou shalt set apart unto the LORD all that openeth the matrix, and every firstling that cometh of a beast which thou hast; the males shall be the LORD'S.
All that openeth the matrix is mine; and every firstling among thy cattle, whether ox or sheep, that is male.
Num 3:12
And I, behold, I have taken the Levites from among the children of Israel instead of all the firstborn that openeth the matrix among the children of Israel: therefore the Levites shall be mine;

Every thing that openeth the matrix in all flesh, which they bring unto the LORD, whether it be of men or beasts, shall be thine: nevertheless the firstborn of man shalt thou surely redeem, and the firstling of unclean beasts shalt thou redeem.
corruption_summary: Life in the womb is argued about as a status to be conferred, while Exodus treats the first thing a womb yields as already God's by right.
corruption_paragraphs: The formula all that openeth the matrix is mine settles a question the present age has managed to keep open. The claim in Exodus attaches at birth to what the womb yields, and it attaches by divine right rather than by human recognition — no ceremony confers it, no parent bestows it, and Israel's only option is to redeem what is already the LORD's. That is a categorically different framework from one in which value is granted to human life once it has met a threshold set by someone else.

The redemption clause is the gospel in miniature. Numbers 18:15 says that every thing that openeth the matrix shall be the priest's, and immediately adds, nevertheless the firstborn of man shalt thou surely redeem. The claim is not waived; it is satisfied. Israel's sons lived because a price was paid and a substitute accepted, and Luke records Mary and Joseph bringing the Lord Jesus to Jerusalem under this very law, quoting it: every male that openeth the womb shall be called holy to the Lord.
roots_summary: Hebrew rechem (H7358), womb; the phrase peter rechem, that which openeth the womb, is the technical term for the firstborn claim.
roots_lines: Hebrew rechem (H7358) — womb, matrix; Exodus 13:12, 34:19.
Hebrew peter (H6363) — that which first opens; the firstborn of man or beast.
Hebrew bekor (H1060) — firstborn; the person the claim falls upon.
Hebrew padah (H6299) — to redeem, to ransom; the firstborn of man shalt thou surely redeem.
Hebrew qadash (H6942) — to sanctify, set apart; Exodus 13:2, sanctify unto me all the firstborn.
usage: “All that openeth the matrix is mine” — the claim stated without condition.
“All the firstborn of my children I redeem” — the claim satisfied, not waived.
“I have taken the Levites… instead of all the firstborn” — substitution written into the law.

etymology: Old French garnir, to furnish or fit out. The KJV uses it for adornment at the largest scale — the heavens — and the smallest, an empty swept room.
biblical_def: Garnished means adorned or furnished out, and Scripture uses it at both ends of the scale. Solomon's temple: “And he garnished the house with precious stones for beauty: and the gold was gold of Parvaim” (2Ch 3:6). The created heavens: “By his spirit he hath garnished the heavens; his hand hath formed the crooked serpent” (Job 26:13). The consummated city: “And the foundations of the wall of the city were garnished with all manner of precious stones. The first foundation was jasper; the second, sapphire” (Rev 21:19). And then the Lord's warning, where the word turns cold: “Then he saith, I will return into my house from whence I came out; and when he is come, he findeth it empty, swept, and garnished” (Mat 12:44). Luke reports the same parable: “And when he cometh, he findeth it swept and garnished” (Luk 11:25). A house may be beautifully appointed and still be empty, and in that parable the emptiness is the whole danger. The unclean spirit does not return to a filthy house. He returns to a tidy one.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines garnish as to adorn; to decorate with appendages; to set off; to furnish or fit out.
webster_full: GARNISH, v.t. To adorn; to decorate with appendages; to set off.
2. To fit with fetters; a cant term.
3. To furnish; to supply.
GARNISHED, pp. Adorned; decorated; furnished.
scriptures: And he garnished the house with precious stones for beauty: and the gold was gold of Parvaim.
By his spirit he hath garnished the heavens; his hand hath formed the crooked serpent.
Then he saith, I will return into my house from whence I came out; and when he is come, he findeth it empty, swept, and garnished.
And the foundations of the wall of the city were garnished with all manner of precious stones. The first foundation was jasper; the second, sapphire; the third, a chalcedony; the fourth, an emerald;
corruption_summary: Moral reformation without regeneration is mistaken for conversion; Christ calls that condition empty, swept, and garnished.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 12:44 is one of the most searching sentences in the Gospels for respectable people. The house is not described as dirty. It is empty, swept, and garnished — reformed, tidied, made presentable. And that is precisely the condition in which the unclean spirit returns with seven others worse than himself, so that the last state of that man is worse than the first. Reformation that removes a vice without installing a new Tenant leaves a furnished vacancy.

This is the standing rebuke to every gospel that consists of behaviour management — the sermon that gets a man to stop drinking and never gets him to Christ, the ministry that measures success in habits broken. Scripture's remedy is not a cleaner house but an occupied one: Christ dwelling in the heart by faith. Job and Revelation show what God does with a place He means to fill; He garnishes the heavens and the foundations of the city, and He is there.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsaphah (H6823), to overlay or adorn; shiphrah (H8235), fairness, in Job's garnished heavens; Greek kosmeo (G2885), to put in order, to adorn — the root of cosmos.
roots_lines: Greek kosmeo (G2885) — to adorn, to set in order; Matthew 12:44, Luke 11:25, Revelation 21:19.
Hebrew tsaphah (H6823) — to overlay, to adorn; 2 Chronicles 3:6.
Hebrew shiphrah (H8235) — beauty, fairness; Job 26:13, the garnished heavens.
Greek scholazo (G4980) — to be empty, unoccupied; the fatal word beside garnished.
Greek sesaromenon — swept; from saroo (G4563), the tidying that is not conversion.
usage: “By his spirit he hath garnished the heavens” — adornment at the scale of creation.
“He findeth it empty, swept, and garnished” — the tidy house is the dangerous one.
“Garnished with all manner of precious stones” — the city God adorns and inhabits.

pos: adj. (softly reared; pampered; unaccustomed to hardship; Hebrew 'anog, rak)
etymology: Latin delicatus, giving pleasure, luxurious. In the KJV it never means fragile by nature; it means softened by ease, and it is normally the prelude to a judgment.
biblical_def: Scripture's delicate man or woman is not frail by constitution but softened by comfort, and the word almost always stands in a siege or a captivity. Moses warns of what famine will do to the gentlest among them: “So that the man that is tender among you, and very delicate, his eye shall be evil toward his brother, and toward the wife of his bosom” (Deu 28:54), and the companion verse is worse: “The tender and delicate woman among you, which would not adventure to set the sole of her foot upon the ground for delicateness and tenderness, her eye shall be evil toward the husband of her bosom” (Deu 28:56). Isaiah says it to Babylon: “Come down, and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon, sit on the ground: there is no throne, O daughter of the Chaldeans: for thou shalt no more be called tender and delicate” (Isa 47:1). Jeremiah says it to Judah: “I have likened the daughter of Zion to a comely and delicate woman” (Jer 6:2), and an army is at the gate by the next verse. Micah mourns the children of it: “Make thee bald, and poll thee for thy delicate children… for they are gone into captivity from thee” (Mic 1:16). Ease is not neutral. Deuteronomy 28 says it does not survive contact with hunger.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines delicate as pleasing to the senses; nice; soft; effeminate; and, of persons, tender, unable to endure hardship.
webster_full: DELICATE, a. Of an agreeable flavor; pleasing to the taste; as a delicate viand.
2. Nice; pleasing to the senses; fine.
3. Soft; effeminate; not able to endure hardship; as a delicate person.
4. Requiring nice handling; as a delicate question.
scriptures: So that the man that is tender among you, and very delicate, his eye shall be evil toward his brother, and toward the wife of his bosom, and toward the remnant of his children which he shall leave:

The tender and delicate woman among you, which would not adventure to set the sole of her foot upon the ground for delicateness and tenderness, her eye shall be evil toward the husband of her bosom, and toward her son, and toward her daughter,
Isa 47:1
Come down, and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon, sit on the ground: there is no throne, O daughter of the Chaldeans: for thou shalt no more be called tender and delicate.
Jer 6:2
I have likened the daughter of Zion to a comely and delicate woman.
corruption_summary: Comfort is treated as a neutral condition, while Deuteronomy makes softness the thing that fails first and worst under pressure.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 28:54–56 is unbearable to read and impossible to misunderstand. The tender and delicate woman who would not set the sole of her foot upon the ground is the one whose eye becomes evil toward her own children in the siege. Moses is not saying that gentle people are secretly cruel. He is saying that a soul kept from every hardship has no reserves, and that when the hardship comes anyway it discovers what was never built. This is the plainest biblical argument against raising children, or churches, on comfort.

The therapeutic instinct of the present age is to treat every discomfort as an injury to be prevented, and it produces exactly the person Deuteronomy describes. Scripture's alternative is not harshness but training — no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness. Hebrews assumes hardship is coming and asks what it will find; Deuteronomy shows what it finds in the delicate.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'anog (H6028), dainty, delicate, softened by luxury; rak (H7390), tender, soft; 'anugah, the delicateness of Deuteronomy 28:56.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'anog (H6028) — delicate, dainty; Deuteronomy 28:54, 28:56, Isaiah 47:1.
Hebrew rak (H7390) — tender, soft; paired with delicate in every warning.
Hebrew 'anugah (H6026) — delicateness; the state, not the temperament.
Hebrew ta'anug (H8588) — luxury, exquisite delight; Micah 1:16, the delicate children.
Hebrew bath-tsiyon — daughter of Zion; likened to a comely and delicate woman, Jeremiah 6:2.
usage: “The tender and delicate woman among you” — and the siege is the subject.
“Thou shalt no more be called tender and delicate” — said to Babylon on the ground.
“Poll thee for thy delicate children” — ease does not travel into captivity.

etymology: From skill, Old Norse skil, discernment or distinction, with -ful. The KJV spelling keeps one l. Scripture ties skill to wisdom rather than to talent.
biblical_def: Scripture is unembarrassed about skill, and it praises it in soldiers, singers, and craftsmen alike. Of the trans-Jordan tribes: “men able to bear buckler and sword, and to shoot with bow, and skilful in war, were four and forty thousand seven hundred and threescore” (1Ch 5:18). David appoints the temple workforce with the assumption that competence is a spiritual qualification: “there shall be with thee for all manner of workmanship every willing skilful man, for any manner of service” (1Ch 28:21). Huram's master workman is described at length: “his father was a man of Tyre, skilful to work in gold, and in silver, in brass, in iron, in stone, and in timber, in purple, in blue, and in fine linen, and in crimson; also to grave any manner of graving” (2Ch 2:14). Daniel and his companions were “skilful in all wisdom, and cunning in knowledge, and understanding science” (Dan 1:4). The word is not always a compliment — Ezekiel speaks of brutish men “skilful to destroy” (Eze 21:31). Skill is a power, and like every power it takes the moral character of the hand that holds it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines skilful as knowing; well versed in any art; hence, dextrous; able in practice; expert.
webster_full: SKILFUL, a. Knowing; well versed in any art; hence, dextrous; able in practice.
2. Well versed in practice; expert; as a skilful mechanic.
SKILL, n. The familiar knowledge of any art or science, united with readiness and dexterity in execution or performance.
scriptures: The sons of Reuben, and the Gadites, and half the tribe of Manasseh, of valiant men, men able to bear buckler and sword, and to shoot with bow, and skilful in war, were four and forty thousand seven hundred and threescore, that went out to the war.

And, behold, the courses of the priests and the Levites, even they shall be with thee for all the service of the house of God: and there shall be with thee for all manner of workmanship every willing skilful man, for any manner of service: also the princes and all the people will be wholly at thy commandment.

The son of a woman of the daughters of Dan, and his father was a man of Tyre, skilful to work in gold, and in silver, in brass, in iron, in stone, and in timber, in purple, in blue, and in fine linen, and in crimson; also to grave any manner of graving, and to find out every device which shall be put to him, with thy cunning men, and with the cunning men of my lord David thy father.
Dan 1:4

Children in whom was no blemish, but well favoured, and skilful in all wisdom, and cunning in knowledge, and understanding science, and such as had ability in them to stand in the king's palace, and whom they might teach the learning and the tongue of the Chaldeans.
corruption_summary: Competence is treated as unspiritual and sincerity as sufficient, while Scripture names craftsmanship a gift of the Spirit and staffs the temple with it.
corruption_paragraphs: A persistent piety holds that skill is worldly and that God prefers the willing amateur. Exodus 31 destroys it outright: the LORD says of Bezaleel that He has filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship. The first man in Scripture explicitly said to be filled with the Spirit was a craftsman, and what the Spirit produced in him was competence. David's standard for temple service is the same — every willing skilful man. Willing and skilful, not one instead of the other.

Ezekiel 21:31 keeps this from becoming a simple endorsement. Brutish men are called skilful to destroy. Skill amplifies whatever it serves, which is why Scripture never commends it in isolation but always attaches it to wisdom — chokmah, the same word rendered wisdom in Proverbs and skill in Exodus. Competence severed from the fear of the LORD is not neutral; it is a sharper instrument in the same fallen hand.
roots_summary: Hebrew chakam (H2450), wise, skilful — one word for both; bin (H995), to discern; maskil (H7919), to act with insight and so to prosper.
roots_lines: Hebrew chakam (H2450) — wise, skilful; 2 Chronicles 2:14, of the craftsman of Tyre.
Hebrew chokmah (H2451) — wisdom, skill; rendered both ways, Exodus 31:3 and Proverbs 1:2.
Hebrew bin (H995) — to discern, be skilful; 1 Chronicles 15:22.
Hebrew maskil (H7919) — to act prudently, to prosper by insight; Daniel 1:4.
Hebrew melakah (H4399) — workmanship; the sphere skill is exercised in, 1 Chronicles 28:21.
usage: “Every willing skilful man, for any manner of service” — both words, not either.
“Skilful to work in gold, and in silver, in brass, in iron” — the temple was built by experts.
“Skilful to destroy” — the same competence in a brutish hand.

pos: n. pl. (devices, contrivances of the heart; Hebrew chishshabon, ma'alal)
etymology: Latin invenire, to find out or come upon. In the KJV it usually means what man finds out for himself, and Ecclesiastes uses it for the whole history of that search.
biblical_def: Inventions in the KJV are usually not machines but devices of the heart. Ecclesiastes gives the summary verdict on the human race: “Lo, this only have I found, that God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions” (Ecc 7:29). That single sentence holds both the doctrine of a good creation and the doctrine of the fall, and it locates the fall in a search. The psalmist uses the word for the wilderness rebellion: “Thus they provoked him to anger with their inventions: and the plague brake in upon them” (Psa 106:29), and again, “Thus were they defiled with their own works, and went a whoring with their own inventions” (Psa 106:39). Even forgiveness is set beside it: “Thou answeredst them, O LORD our God: thou wast a God that forgavest them, though thou tookest vengeance of their inventions” (Psa 99:8). Yet the word is not condemned in itself. Wisdom claims a good kind: “I wisdom dwell with prudence, and find out knowledge of witty inventions” (Pro 8:12). Contrivance is a creaturely power. Turned toward God's ends it is wisdom; turned toward our own it is Ecclesiastes 7:29.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines invention as the action or operation of finding out something new; the contrivance of that which did not before exist; also, forgery, fiction.
webster_full: INVENTION, n. The action or operation of finding out something new; the contrivance of that which did not before exist.
2. That which is invented; a contrivance; a device.
3. Forgery; fiction.
4. The power of inventing; that skill or ingenuity which is or may be employed in contriving any thing new.
scriptures: Ecc 7:29
Lo, this only have I found, that God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions.
Thus they provoked him to anger with their inventions: and the plague brake in upon them.
Thus were they defiled with their own works, and went a whoring with their own inventions.
Pro 8:12
I wisdom dwell with prudence, and find out knowledge of witty inventions.
corruption_summary: Human progress is treated as self-evidently upward, while Ecclesiastes files the whole search under what man sought out after God had made him upright.
corruption_paragraphs: Ecclesiastes 7:29 is the shortest anthropology in Scripture and it is fatal to the doctrine of inevitable progress. God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions. The original condition was uprightness; everything since has been contrivance. That does not make invention wicked — Proverbs 8:12 has wisdom finding out witty inventions — but it does destroy the assumption that the direction of human ingenuity is naturally upward. The tools have improved; the heart that seeks out inventions has not.

Psalm 106 shows what the inventions of a covenant people look like in practice: not technology but worship of their own devising, and the plague breaking in upon them. The Hebrew word is close kin to the term for reasonings and schemes. This is the regulative principle stated from the negative side — when the LORD has not commanded a thing in His worship, the thing offered is an invention, and Scripture's record of what He does with those is not encouraging.
roots_summary: Hebrew chishshabon (H2810), a device or contrivance; ma'alal (H4611), a deed or practice; mezimmah (H4209), a purpose or discretion — good or evil by its object.
roots_lines: Hebrew chishshabon (H2810) — invention, device; Ecclesiastes 7:29.
Hebrew ma'alal (H4611) — doing, practice, invention; Psalm 99:8, 106:29.
Hebrew mezimmah (H4209) — discretion, device; Proverbs 8:12, the witty inventions of wisdom.
Hebrew yashar (H3477) — upright; the condition man was made in.
Hebrew baqash (H1245) — to seek out; the verb of the fall in Ecclesiastes 7:29.
usage: “God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions” — the fall as a search.
“They provoked him to anger with their inventions” — worship of our own devising.
“Knowledge of witty inventions” — contrivance under wisdom's hand.
